title: Declaration and memory allocation
concept: The moment you declare a variable, it takes up space in memory (but not initialized).

steps.title: Include header files
steps.explanation:
`#include <stdio.h>` imports declarations for using standard input/output functions such as `printf`.

You just need to remember the essentials: without this line you will get a compilation error when using `printf`.

steps.title: main function definition
steps.explanation:
`int main()` is the program entry point. When execution begins, a main stack frame is created and local variables are stored in this frame.

At this stage we haven't declared any local variables yet, so all we have is a frame.

steps.title: variable declaration
steps.explanation:
`int a;` only reserves memory space and does not insert a value.

So `a` is a garbage value, and reading it can give unpredictable results. In general, it is a safe practice to use initialization together, such as `int a = 0;`.

steps.title: Garbage Value
steps.explanation:
If you print `a` uninitialized, the results may vary depending on the execution environment.

This is Undefined Behavior and can cause bugs that are very difficult to debug. The conclusion is simple: initialize local variables as soon as they are declared.
steps.stdout: Value of a: 21845 (example, varies per execution)

quiz.question: When a variable is declared in C language, which of the following is the value contained in the variable?
quiz.explanation:
Automatic initialization only occurs for global or static variables.
If local variables within a function are not initialized, they will contain garbage values.

misconceptions.correct: Local variables never automatically become zero.
misconceptions.why: This is because we believe that initializing it to 0 every time is a waste of performance (performance is top priority in C language).

keyTakeaway: Creating a variable creates memory space. However, I have to enter the value myself.
